findings.highlight: An hour’s walk to the mountain.
findings.evidenceJa: ここから山に向かって歩くこと一時間
findings.governingReading: Ryuudou Temple lies about an hour’s walk from this point toward the mountain.
findings.explanation: The fragment loses the prospective route relation and reads as an isolated duration.

findings.highlight: Ever since I went there last summer to stay there as mental training.
findings.evidenceJa: 去年の夏、精神修行という事で合宿させてもらって以来か
findings.governingReading: Shirou has not visited since being allowed to stay there for spiritual training last summer.
findings.explanation: The English leaves the temporal relation as a sentence fragment.

findings.governingReading: Shirou concludes that he worried needlessly.
findings.explanation: A natural self-correction becomes an unidiomatic clinical-sounding noun.

findings.highlight: Geez, he’s so serious, so he’s hard to deal with when he gets like this.
findings.evidenceJa: ぶつぶつとお経を唱える生徒会長
findings.governingReading: Issei mutters sutras to himself after ordering himself to reject lust.
findings.explanation: The English adds a full evaluative narration sentence absent from the active Japanese.

findings.highlight: I wish to purify myself more
findings.evidenceJa: より精進したいと思う
findings.governingReading: Issei says his training is insufficient and he intends to apply himself more diligently.
findings.explanation: The English turns continued religious discipline into purification of the self.

findings.highlight: as he disappears into the back of the town
findings.governingReading: Issei leaves behind a sharp “Katsu!” and disappears deeper into town.
findings.explanation: The characteristic final exclamation is omitted, flattening the end of his comic religious performance.

findings.highlight: I’ll talk to her about what I heard from Shinji after Sakura and Fuji-nee go home
findings.evidenceJa: 慎二から聞いた話は、桜と藤ねえが帰ってから
findings.governingReading: Shirou will discuss Shinji’s information after Sakura and Fuji-nee have left; the addressee is unstated here.
findings.explanation: The English supplies a female singular confidant before the source names one.

findings.highlight: I’m talking about the taste of the food
findings.evidenceJa: わたしが言っているのは料理の味じゃありません
findings.governingReading: Rin explicitly says that she is not discussing the food’s taste.
findings.explanation: The English drops the negation and states the opposite of her correction.

findings.evidenceJa: 五人分の特製炊き込みご飯
findings.governingReading: The special mixed rice is explicitly a five-person quantity.
findings.explanation: The quantity anchoring the later excess-food joke disappears.

findings.governingReading: The short sound marks tableware clattering while the group eats.
findings.explanation: The English changes a utensil or dish sound into chewing, flattening the alternating meal rhythm.

findings.highlight: It’s not a cask, it’s a pot
findings.governingReading: Shirou corrects Saber: the vessel is an ohitsu, a rice tub, not a barrel.
findings.explanation: The correction lands on the generic “pot,” weakening the concrete object at the center of the joke.

findings.highlight: using citrus instead of fried things for its aroma
findings.evidenceJa: 柚子で香りをとってる
findings.governingReading: Sakura notices that yuzu supplies fragrance in place of an oily ingredient.
findings.explanation: The English generalizes yuzu to citrus and distorts an oily ingredient into “fried things.”

findings.evidenceJa: 昨日今日やってきた人
findings.governingReading: Fuji-nee possessively dismisses people who only recently entered the household.
findings.explanation: Calling Rin and Saber strangers hardens a temporal, territorial complaint into denial of acquaintance.

findings.evidenceJa: セイバーは我関せずで飯食ってる
findings.governingReading: Saber keeps eating with an air that the commotion has nothing to do with her.
findings.explanation: The English drops her pointed detachment, erasing one of the three contrasted reactions.

findings.highlight: I don’t want it accidentally trespassing into human society
findings.evidenceJa: 人間社会に間違って乱入してこないでほしい
findings.governingReading: Shirou jokingly treats Fuji-nee as a wild tiger that should not stray into human society.
findings.explanation: The pronoun “it” literalizes and dehumanizes the metaphor instead of sustaining the mock address to Taiga.
